Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When the committee rose previously we had reached resolution 601. Architectural branch-
Acquisition, construction and improvements of public buildings-
Construction, acquisition, major repairs and improvements of, and plans and sites for, public; buildings listed in the details of the estimates, provided that treasury board may increase or decrease the amount within the vote to be expended on individual listed projects-further amounts required-
601. Ottawa, $1,732,666.

Mr. Chairman, this item is to complete payment for the expropriation of a property at the corner of Bay and Wellington streets, and for the acquisition of a former seminary building. The further amount required to complete payment for the seminary building is $1,576,666. I have been looking through the estimates, and while this item is to complete payment may I say I have always understood that the purpose of supplementary estimates was to tidy up odds and ends here and there. In June last year an amount of $2 million was voted of which $1 million was for practically the same item. Here we have an item of over $1,500,000 to tidy up things, and I do not see any reason why the government has brought in this item at this time as a supplementary estimate. I have newspaper clippings here to prove that the seminary building has been under the control of the government for some three years. I want to find out why this item was brought in as a supplementary estimate and not as an ordinary estimate in the regular routine of providing for government requirements. This matter is not new. It has been before parliament for some three or four years. It was a new building, and there is no doubt in the world that the mounted police certainly needed new quarters. They were spread all over the city of Ottawa and had no real home. Why this building has been purchased when, even during the time it was occupied under a rental basis, it was found to be inadequate for mounted police purposes,


I do not understand. Yet, the government has gone ahead with the purchase of this property.
In the Ottawa Journal of May 21, 1951, we find this:
New seminary being acquired by government.
The new seminary today was slated to become headquarters for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
Some R.C.M.P. staffs in the city are reported getting ready to move into the building about August 1.
No official figure on the deal could be obtained. It was understood that final details still had to be ironed out between federal and diocesan authorities.
The seminary, just now nearing completion, cost almost $4 million. It is located in Overbrook.
The large building will provide badly needed space for the R.C.M.P.'s expansion program, which will see new laboratories and training facilities all gathered under one roof.
The R.C.M.P. now is spread over the city in the following locations:
Then there is a list of the locations given.
Then again on September 12, 1952, there was an article in the Ottawa Citizen headed "Seminary as Mounties' HQ". It reads as follows:
A sprawling building in Overbrook that was built as a seminary but never occupied will become the headquarters of Canada's federal police starting next month, it was learned today.
Millions of fingerprints, thousands of records-
And so on. There follows a list of things to be moved.
It will concentrate under one roof offices and divisions which have been scattered all over Ottawa. It will free about six floors of the justice building on Wellington street and smaller offices in a score of locations throughout the downtown area.
All R.C.M.P. divisions except "A" division, the local police detachment and the training division at Rockcliffe will move to the seminary. "A" division will move across from the Canadian Bank Note building into the justice building to occupy some of the space that will become vacant. The training division and the crime detection laboratory will stay at Rockcliffe barracks.
The move will rank with that of the dominion bureau of statistics in magnitude. It will take several weeks to complete owing to the mass of fingerprints and records that must be transferred. Divisions will be moved in sequence to their new offices.
Evidently the building was occupied on a rental basis at that time, in September of 1952.
In the Ottawa Journal of April, 1953, we find an article headed, "Fournier backs building policy". The article reads in part:
As to the seminary building, Mr. Fournier told the house that this new structure and an additional building which will cost $150,000 "is absolutely necessary for the efficient operation of their headquarters, and to take care of their normal expansion requirements." The smaller building to be put near the huge seminary will have 12,500 feet of floor space.
Evidently the new building was in process of being purchased, that is April 10, 1953.

In the Ottawa Citizen of November 16, 1953, some six months later, we find an article with this heading, "$10 million project; New R.C.M.P. buildings will be built here".
The subheadings are as follows, "Homes, offices for men"; "Have choice of two sites", and the article reads:
A new permanent R.C.M.P. headquarters and housing development is to be built in Ottawa within the next five years at a cost that may run well over $10 million, it was learned today. The force said in its annual report that it is making plans for construction of the new headquarters which will replace its temporary quarters in Overbrook-
This is the new building they are talking about here. The building was rented at that time.
The site has not been picked out, but it may be on land already owned by the government, either south of the Rideau river and not far from the projected Ottawa railway station when it is moved from its present centretown area, or east of the city on the proving ground site at Green's creek which has been mentioned as a possible site for the proposed national defence headquarters.
In any event, officials said, it would not be in or near the centre of the city, but would definitely be in a suburban location.
It will be larger than the present temporary headquarters building, running to around 260,000 square feet of space, and designed to accommodate all branches of the force, including stores which are still located in rented quarters in downtown Ottawa.
Adjoining the new headquarters will be a housing development for members of the force, and shops, stores and other subsidiary buildings.
The present temporary headquarters building was occupied by the force only a few months ago but already is inadequate. Halls and passages are used for filing cases and records and the building is not the most suitable because it was designed originally as a religious centre.
It is held by the Public Works Department on a five-year lease with an option for two more years if required.
"It is definitely hoped that the new headquarters will be ready when the lease runs out", a works department official said today.
That would mean that work would have to start on the new headquarters within two or three years. The site must be approved by the national capital planning committee and the federal district commission, as well as the Public Works Department and the force itself.
Preliminary plans have been submitted by the force to the Public Works Department, and there may be an appropriation in the estimates for the 1954-55 fiscal year to cover the cost of preparing detailed plans.
Once the site is picked, it is expected there will be few delays in proceeding with the plans and the letting of a contract.
That article was written on November 16, 1953, and the building still had not been purchased but was occupied on a rental basis. Even at that time the building was found to be inadequate for a mounted police headquarters. The government decided, after renting it for two or three years, to go ahead and purchase it. I should like to know why the government delayed so long in buying it. If it was suitable and large enough at the 50433-161i
Supply-Public Works
start, it is probably big enough now. The article in the newspapers says it is inadequate. Another question I should like answered is whether or not the rental paid has been applied on the purchase price. Will the Minister of Finance answer that when he has time? I should like to know also why some of this money has not been put in the regular estimates. Is it an attempt to slip it through with appropriations for other buildings in the Ottawa district? It looks as if this was something the government was trying to keep out of sight.
In June, 1954, there was an amount in the supplementary estimates of $1 million for this building, that is a year ago. On June 23, 1954, a question was asked by the hon. member for Kamloops concerning this building, and it appears at page 6575 of Hansard for June 23, 1954:

I have a question or two about this item. I understood that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police were acquiring a large building out here as a new headquarters at a cost of some $6 million.
The amount now mentioned is $6 million, but before that time an amount of $5 million had been mentioned. We would like to know what it is going to cost when the additional building is added. I continue the quotation:
I do not find it listed anywhere under acquisition of buildings, works, land and new equipment, or under the administration item or anywhere else.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am afraid that I cannot assist my hon. friend in that regard. We are the occupants of it as the mounted police, but the purchase of it would be arranged through the Department of Public Works.

That is different from the other
items in the minister's department.
That is another thing I want answered: why make any difference in connection with this building?
Then, on June 25, two days later, there was a question asked by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra which appears at page 6773 of Hansard. It reads as follows:

Why was it necessary to have this amount in the supplementary estimates? It is two-thirds of the total vote. The Department of Public Works is supposed to have the new look, and we understood that they had everything up to date.
They have.

We want evidence of it.
That is what we want, evidence of it.

They are asking for an additional
$2 million for public buildings in Ottawa, in the supplementary estimates.
Why was not at least some of this amount put in the main estimates?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I am told that $1 million is for the seminary and $1 million for property on Wellington street which was expropriated last year.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
I am told that at that time the
decision had not been taken. That is why it had to be brought in with the supplementary estimates.
They had this building. Evidently they knew they were going to buy it. But still the minister's representative said at that time:
I am told that at that time the decision had not been taken. That is why it had to be brought in with the supplementary estimates.
That was last year. Why has this been brought in with the supplementary estimates this year? Why was it not included in the regular estimates? It is about time that this government, in its business activities, would put them out in the open so that people could see them, and not try to mix them up with other buildings, with other moneys invested for the district commission of Ottawa. It looks as if this might be a hidden fixture. It is just another part of the government's secret activities in hiding the estimates that refer to the business done throughout the year.
I do not see why they did not put it through as an order in council. That is one way they have been hiding things for years. I know the official opposition is sick and tired of this kind of business, and I think the people of Canada are getting sick of it, too. I do not see why the Minister of Finance could not have included this in the regular estimates. I do not see why he has coupled it up with something else, and called it money for the district commission, or for Ottawa, or something else. Then it might appear that only $1 million was spent last year. Does this mean that it is costing $6 million, or does it mean that the original purchase price was $5 million? Why has there not been something in the regular estimates either last year or this year?
Carried.

No, it is not carried yet, and it will not be carried for a while. And I am surprised that the hon. member for Fort William is calling "carried" on an item of this kind that has been hidden for some three or four years. He is surely not the man who would stand up for that sort of principle.
I am paying close attention to the hon. member.
I have the floor, and I am making the speech; and if you want to speak, you can speak afterwards.
Thank you.
I would be glad to hear what you have to say about it, if you are a minister of the gospel and a member of the House of Commons.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
Don't bring that into it.
I will bring anything I like into it. I have the floor. And I would like to hear from some of you rubber stamps.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member should confine his remarks to item 601, which is under consideration.

Let the rubber stamps keep quiet, and I will finish my speech. I would like to know the total purchase price, and what it is estimated it will cost when completed. I would like to know why this has not been brought in, in the regular way, in the main estimates rather than leaving it to the supplementary estimates both last year and this year.
There is no doubt about it that, as I said before, the mounted police need new quarters. But I think I have proven that this building is inadequate for them. They needed a new building. Probably it will cost $10 million before we are through. We know that the Hon. Mr. Fournier, when minister of public works, brought in an estimate on one occasion for $140,000 for a building in the city of Ottawa, and before he was through it cost $600,000. So we want to know whether this is going to be the same set-up. This seems to be the way the government is doing business, and I think it is about time they got down to doing it in a straightforward and frank manner, so that the people would know what they are doing.

Mr. Chairman, I have no quarrel at the moment over the price being paid for this building, but I would like to make reference to the manner in which it is being purchased. At page 3648 of Hansard for	April	9, 1953, the	hon. member	for
Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green), in questioning the then minister of public works, Mr. Fournier, had this to say:
Is	there	any intention	to expropriate	the
seminary?
In reply the then minister said:
I	would	not give any	inkling as to	that.
Actually tor the space we	get in that building,
I think we are paying a little bit less than we do in the normal unit price over the city. I would not say yes or no. The government has not considered that. We needed space badly for the staff of the mounted police who had been asking for it since the war, and this was the only place that we could get rapidly. We have taken a lease on it for five years. As to the future intention of the government, the matter has not been considered, to my knowledge.
On May 22, 1954, I find this in the Ottawa Citizen:
The government Friday provided $1 million in supplementary estimates for the current fiscal year

toward acquisition of the Overbrook seminary building now occupied by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police headquarters.
And on November 30, 1954, the following:
A new concentration of government buildings at Hurdmans Bridge was in prospect today with announcement that the purchase of the seminary there had been completed at a cost of $5 million, the purchase including 114 acres of land.
The seminary now is occupied by the R.C.M.P. as a headquarters and there is no proposal to move the Rockcliffe training establishment or the A division uptown offices from their existing locations . . .
The purchase of the building had been practically decided a year ago but the Public Works Department and the vendors decided to wait until November 1 to have the final arrangements made.
It is mentioned there that in the late spring of 1954, which was a year ago, the government had provided $1 million in the supplementary estimates for the purchase of this building. Then, in the estimates before us at the moment there is an amount of $1,576,666 as payment toward the purchase price of this building. On Friday evening the Minister of Finance stated that this was the final payment. What I wish to know is this: Are any of the payments made by way of rentals for this building included in the purchase price? Are they being applied against the purchase price?
One further question is this: Have any of these payments been estimated for in the regular estimates? If not, when were other requests brought down for the completion of the payments on this building? I must say I have been unable to find them in any of the estimates, other than these two amounts which total something more than $2,500,000.
Finally, let me say that I have no quarrel with the purchase of the building. At the moment I have no quarrel with the price being paid; but I think these payments have been made in an irregular fashion, and not according to the practice of the House of Commons.

Would the Minister of Justice not save a lot of time-and time has already

Supply-Public Works been wasted-if he produced the facts regarding this transaction so that the members of parliament could get the information and transmit it to the public that this deal is open and aboveboard in every respect, instead of taking pot shots at various ministers and getting no definite information? Surely the pressure could be relieved and we could go on to other subjects if the facts were laid before parliament, where they should be given. Are we now to believe that during Mr. Fournier's regime as minister of public works, and the regime of the present Prime Minister when he was minister of justice, something happened and all of a sudden overnight it was realized that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police ought to have a building that would cost millions of dollars? If that is so, then some person in charge of that department at that time was negligent in performing his duties. He should have been well aware of the requirements of the police and should have been preparing for them. He should have known that the department would require a building to house the police adequately. Apparently they had to jump in and buy a building which does not suit the requirements and nobody in this house can get any information about it.
Nobody in the country would ever think of purchasing a building under this method, a building that would be adequate to perform the services as efficiently as one which was designed for the purpose of housing the police. This deal should never be rammed down anybody's throat. We should not be told that we can buy a building already constructed that will meet all of the requirements of the police and enable them to function properly in that building. That is ridiculous. This building must have been purchased because of some unforeseen pressure that there was no other building suitable for the police. How ridiculous that is. Imagine any government or any private corporation functioning in that manner. This government is not prepared to cope with circumstances as they arise from time to time. The situation is that this government either does not know, or knowing, is not doing its job. If they know, then they are ignoring their duty. They suddenly realize that we must purchase this building for $5 million, $7 million, or $8 million. The amount is still unknown. The facts of the transaction are still unknown. If that is the way they are carrying on business, then the public should know what is going on. If we are to get the facts from the Minister of Finance, I would like to hear them. I do not think he can

give us the facts regarding this deal in the few minutes that he has at his disposal.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, out of politeness I have been waiting for all the questions from the other side to be asked at the one time. I did not expect, however, to sit here and be lectured by one who apparently did not pay any attention even to what the members of his own party were saying about the deal.
If I did not pay any attention to them, I know I will not get anything by paying attention to you. I will learn nothing from you.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I agree that the hon. member cannot learn anything from very many people.
You learn nothing; we all know you.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: This transaction is a perfectly simple one.
You are too big for your shoes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
If hon. members had followed the hon. member for Victoria, Ont., they would have heard, I think, a strictly correct chronological statement of what happened, with one exception. This building was being constructed from 1948 on. About 1950 it was decided that the R.C.M.P. who, of course, had need of extra quarters for quite some time and not overnight, as my hon. friend seems to think, would have to be given extra and better quarters. The result was this building- and I am going to telescope for a moment- was rented for the purposes of the R.C.M.P. under negotiations which ran from 1951 and were concluded in 1952. It was not until 1953 that the owner of the property indicated that the property might be for sale. It was not until 1954 that the property was bought, and that is the simple explanation of the timing of the whole transaction.
That also explains why there was no item in the estimates that were prepared a year ago last fall. The explanation as to why it is not in the estimates for the coming year is that we put it in the supplementary estimates for this year to clean it up at this time. It is finished. I do not think there is anything hidden about that. I am sure hon. members will agree with me that this is the normal method of dealing with supplementaries.
Will the minister permit a question? Will he fill in the gap between the first supplementary estimate and the last one?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Yes, I will come to that. At the time that the supplementary estimate was being discussed here last May or June-I think I heard a date of June 22 referred to but I cannot find a reference to it on that date-the first supplementary estimate of a year ago was a sum of money to be used to secure the transaction, if it could be negotiated. I think hon. members will agree, however, that at that point, without a firm agreement, it would not be likely that there would be any indication given in parliament as to what price we would be prepared to pay for the property. Negotiations for the property were continued throughout the summer last year and only completed by a treasury board minute in August of last year. From then on the next step and the only step to be taken is to put a further item in the final supplementaries for the current fiscal year and vote it, and that is what I am asking parliament to do at the moment.
I think I have given the committee the basis of the transaction, but I should like to comment on the price for a moment. 1 notice that the hon. member for Wentworth was not complaining about the purchase price, so I take it, but I notice that the hon. member for Victoria, Ont., and the hon. member for Sim-coe North thought that we ought to have spent $10 million on a new building instead of the $5 million we are spending on this one. I want to warn them that while I was not minister of finance-

Does the minister not think that it is sometimes better to spend $10 million and get $10 million worth than to spend $5 million and not get your value? That is what I said; that was the implication. Do not make statements that are misleading.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
In every expenditure made by the government there is always the problem that if you spend $1 you might not possibly get the most you can hope to get, but if you spend $2 you are sure of getting it. That is a decision that has to be made every time something is purchased, particularly a large property of this kind.
I agree that if the Minister of Public Works were to build a building designed specifically for the R.C.M.P. it would be a better building from the standpoint of the police force; no question about that. The point is: is it worth another $5 million? That is the point, and I suggest that in this case-
Are you paying $5 million for this or $6 million? How much would the other building cost that would make it a $10 million building?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I am not familiar with the expenditure on any other building that is being built. I have not an estimate for this
Supply-Public Works and I do not know. I do know the purchase price for this building which is $5 million.

I asked the minister to fill in the gap between the first $1 million in the supplementary estimates and this amount of $1,500,000. There is a difference of nearly $2,500,000 that has to be accounted for.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I thought my hon. friend was referring to the time rather than the money. In every public works vote for a province there is an item which can be used or transferred to permit the construction of buildings that can be completed in that one year when other items are not completed. We have transferred $2,500,000 from that fund toward the purchase price of this building. In doing so we saved interest on the purchase price and that is why it was transferred.
In what year was that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: This would be in the normal estimates for the current year. No money was paid on this building until the calendar year 1954.

The minister has suggested a figure of $10 million for a properly designed building. I never suggested any figure whatever. I merely suggested and said that in my opinion the requirements of the police should have been known over a period of years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: They were.

Long before this building was purchased a concrete idea of their requirements or a near-concrete idea should have been formulated. Therefore the government should have inquired into the cost of a building, whether it be $1 million, $2 million, $5 million, $10 million or $20 million. That figure should have been arrived at as a comparison figure between the cost of building a building suitable for the requirements of the police and any other. They should have had that figure to compare with the price they paid for this building which the minister admits does not meet the requirements fully.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I did not say that.
But you agreed that if a building had been designed for the purposes of the police it probably would have been a better building.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: For $10 million it certainly would have been.
Would you suggest that you might even have improved it for $5 million over the same figure?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I did not suggest that.

Supply-Public Works

Is it not possible, leaving out studding the building with diamonds, that it might have been better even at $5 million if it had been planned for the purpose? Your answer to that is simply yes. I am sure it would have been better at $5 million if properly planned. Is that right? You will not concede that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Of course not. After considering this building and the use to which it could be put, we purchased it. We think it is a good building for the purpose. I quite agree that if we had hired an architect and told him to design a building for the R.C.M.P. he could have designed one which probably would have had more outside entrances, probably a back door for motor cars to come into the building and probably a larger mess hall for the sergeants. But we cannot afford these things in some cases.
The minister says "We cannot afford these things." This is one of the first instances I have ever known this government to say "We cannot afford these things."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: You have heard it many times.

Since the government has lost the support of the Vancouver Sun they are probably getting down to earth and giving consideration to these things. They are afraid of the signs right across this country. The minister says that he has never had an estimate placed before him of the cost of a building adequate for the use of the police and then he says that we cannot afford these things. They cannot afford it even if it costs less than $5 million. That is a fine admission from the Minister of Finance of the Dominion of Canada.

I should like to refer specifically to the question of cost, and perhaps the minister would be good enough to help us. I understand from a previous question that the usable space of this building is 229,500 square feet, and a rental of $370,000 a year seems to be reasonable. However, the purchase price would appear to work out at about $22.50 a square foot. Could the minister indicate if this building is completely air-conditioned, does it have all these fine finishes such as terrazzo floors, does it have a modern type of heating and cooling system? Perhaps the minister could give us some information on that because this would seem to be an outside price. I understand that architects consider that they can provide the best type of accommodation with all these facilities I am speaking of for somewhere between $15 and $20 per square foot. As the hon. member for Simcoe North has said, there

must have been a few diamonds in it if you are going to be able to squeeze it up any higher than that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I warn the hon. member that the average cost of these items he mentioned should not be applied to the city of Ottawa. If he confines himself to asking whether or not these costs are average for Ottawa we will be able to find the information for him. The practice has been for the Department of Public Works to obtain at least two valuations of a building before it is purchased and that practice was followed in this case. We obtained two valuations, one of $4,491,750 and the other $5,386,242, and the purchase price was $5 million. Both firms are well known for their competence in making valuations and I think it will be found that the building is well worth $5 million.
I quite agree with the hon. member for Simcoe North that if ten years ago we had gone to work on a plan we could have planned for a perfect R.C.M.P. building, but in 1954 we had to decide whether we should build a building for the R.C.M.P. We probably might have spent the $10 million that the hon. member for Victoria, Ont., mentioned. But the building would not have been ready for another three or four years. This building is ready. It has a value to that extent that we would not be able to be in a building that we built until three or four years from now.
Do I understand from the minister that building costs in this area are generally considerably higher than they would be, say, in cities of comparable size in the province of Ontario?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I have always understood that building costs in Ottawa were slightly higher.
That situation might be caused by the fact that the government was prepared and willing to pay slightly more.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I think it is caused by the terrain.

I understand that there was an option. I understand that this building could have continued to be rented under an option during this period when plans might have been drawn and a building quite acceptable to the R.C.M.P. could have been constructed. Is that right?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I do not quite understand.
There was an option to renew, at the same rental, the lease that was in existence covering the building?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes. The lease was for five years with an option of renewing it for two years.
What I mean is this. Would that have been adequate time to construct a building according to plans and specifications which would have met R.C.M.P. requirements?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No; not from last year. We could not have had a building of this kind ready for three years from last year, with the building difficulties we have in Ottawa.
Is the building complete now?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes. We have been in it for three years.

I understand that you have been in it; but sometimes you go into these buildings when they are not completed. What I am anxious to know is whether this is the final, complete price of the whole business.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, as far as I know. I have been looking in this coming year's estimates and while I have not been able to run through all the items while we have been talking here, I do not see any. There may be additions such as garages and the like. But there is no substantial building going on, so far as I know. Certainly there is nothing here except completion of the purchase price of the main building.

As to the two figures which the minister quoted as having been given by reputable firms as to the value, there is a difference of nearly $900,000. Was one estimate to be for sale and the other for purchase? That is a rather broad spread, it seems to me, in the valuations made by reputable firms on a building of a value of about $5 million.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I think there is not a difference of $900,000 in their valuations; there is a difference of about $400,000.

Not in the
figures the minister read out.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I beg your pardon. That is right. The difference is about $900,000.
Does the minister not think that is a rather -broad spread in valuation on a $5 million building?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I am not in the business. These are two companies which have done a considerable amount of this work for us. I would suppose that nearly a million dollars in five is probably quite a considerable variation. At the same time I would not want to say that these people do not know what they are doing.
Supply-Public Works

Some short time ago I understood the minister to say that about $2,500,000 of this amount was used from appropriations that had not been used by the Department of Public Works for some other building or buildings?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is right.

What I want to know is this. Is it common practice for the Department of Public Works to use moneys that have been allocated to certain specific buildings; that is, instead of building those buildings, to use the money for some other building without those buildings ever appearing in the estimates at any time, and without their being mentioned by the government in any part of the picture?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No. That is not the practice. In fact, it would be contrary to the financial practice and to the Financial Administration Act. When parliament passed this first $1 million item last spring, parliament authorized the purchase of this building. Thereafter it was in order to allocate funds on hand to the purchase of that building.
What funds?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The funds that were in the unused portion of the public works vote of last year.
What were those votes from which that $2,500,000 was taken? What buildings were those votes specifically for?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The Ottawa grant is usually a lump sum which is set out, of course, in the original estimates. That is true of all the provinces. The money is gathered together and listed under provincial items; and you can transfer from any unspent money within a province, if you will.

Will the minister tell me what that money was allocated for when it was voted by parliament a year ago? Parliament apparently was asked to vote X dollars for buildings in Ottawa. Did not the minister know for what buildings that money was to be allocated? If so, what buildings were dropped?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
No buildings were dropped. I do not want hon. members to understand that the treasury board or the Department of Public Works arbitrarily decides, after a vote in the house, that building X will not be built but that building Y will be built. That is not what is done. If the progress of building X has not used up the amount of money which has been allocated to it, the unspent balance may be used to build the other building. That is what is done here.

Supply-Public Works

We have heard a great deal about this mythical treasury board which scrutinizes so carefully every government expenditure. Treasury board apparently passed X dollars for the acquisition or the building of buildings in Ottawa. I want to know what particular building or buildings treasury board approved in this expenditure of X dollars which afterwards was diverted to the purchase of this building.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I perhaps misled my hon. friend. I did not suggest that there was any one particular building in Ottawa about which the item was underspent. I did say as to the province of Ontario that if your provincial sum is underspent, you can allocate within the province. When it comes before treasury board, it comes in the form of a recommendation that a sum-$2,500,000 in this case- might be used towards the purchase price of this building; and attached to it is a certificate that the moneys allocated for the province are sufficient to provide for this payment having in mind the progress of other various works.
Can the minister say at what date that decision was made?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes. A while ago I said August, 1954.
August, 1954? That was after we voted the estimate.
I should like to go over the dates again with the minister. I understood him to say that this seminary building was under construction from the year 1948 on. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.
The hon. member for Victoria, Ont., read from a press dispatch a statement that the building had cost under $4 million. Is that figure correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I have not that figure.
I beg the minister's pardon?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I do not keep the clippings. I do not know whether that was in the press dispatch or not.
The minister has no information as to what the building cost in the first place? Is that right?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We did not build it. I would not know what it cost.
Then apparently in 1952 the government entered into a five-year lease of the building?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is right.
At a rental of $370,000 a year or just a little bit over $1,000 a day. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is right.

Then for how long did the government pay this rental of $370,000 a
year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: My understanding is that the rental was paid down to the date of the purchase which was, as I say, last year and that the purchase price then bore interest from then on, and we would pay interest and not rental.
Then it was not part of the agreement that the moneys paid by way of rental would apply on the purchase price?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No.
How much rent was paid altogether for the building?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I do not know whether that has been adjusted. Total payments for rental to March 10, 1954, were $449,166.62. I take it that was the day on which there was a firm offer made by the owner of the property.
What date was that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

speechtext: So that on March 10, 1954, the government made a firm offer to purchase the building.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No, they made a firm offer to us that they would sell.
What was paid from that date in March, 1954, until the date the purchase went through?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Nothing was paid until after the $1 million vote was put through the house on the supplementary estimates early last summer. Since that time we have paid $3,500,000.
Did I not understand the minister to say interest was paid from the time the building was offered for sale by the owner? Is that right?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is right.
How much interest did the government pay?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am sorry, I did not understand my hon. friend. The bill for interest will of course be adjusted when we complete final payment. We expect that will run to $56,666 at 5 per cent.
First of all there was $449,000 odd paid for rent. Then there was $66,000-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

speechtext:
Then there is $56,000 for
interest.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Right.
The minister said something about the building being offered for sale in March. At what price did the owners offer it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Five million dollars.
They offered it then at $5 million, and apparently in June of 1954 there was a vote of $1 million placed in the supplementary estimates. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Right.
-and applied it on this purchase.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Is it Ottawa or Ontario?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Ottawa.
Can the minister tell us whether he is referring to vote No. 369 under the Department of Public Works, which was for $10,640,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is right.

The details of that vote are found at page 442 of last year's estimates, and they include roughly 20 different buildings in Ottawa, each of which has a figure placed opposite it. Apparently the government just picked $2J million out of that vote. Is that what happened?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is right.
Why was something not put either in the original estimate for last year or in the supplementary estimates which were dealt with in June-
Or in the regular estimates this year.

-or in the regular estimates for the fiscal year which starts the day after tomorrow, rather than taking $2J million, half the total cost of this building, from this vote for other buildings so that there was not the slightest possible chance of any member of parliament being able to trace that vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The answer is of course the one I have already made, that the time factor is involved. We did not have an offer from the owners that they would sell the property at the time these estimates were being prepared. My hon. friend would have been the first to suggest to the government we
Supply-Public Works should not put an item in the blue book for a building that we had no idea was for sale. The first occasion on which we could bring it before parliament was on the presentation of the first supplementaries to last year's estimates, namely, in late May or early June, because at that time we had an intimation from these people that they would sell at the given price. Far from there being any secrecy about the matter, we bring it to the attention of parliament at the earliest possible moment we can in the ordinary and everyday way. Parliament approved of the purchase by voting $1 million in last year's supplementaries. That is all. It could not have been done in any better way, if I may say so.
Yes, but at that time I think the house was not told what the total purchase price would be. I may be wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I think you are perfectly right, but the reason is that the government had not in fact agreed to purchase the property at $5 million. At that time the offer was outstanding but had not been accepted and we were in the process of trying to negotiate the purchase price. Hon. members will understand that under those circumstances we would not want to be indicating what our view was about the value of the property. It is true that at a later time we did complete the purchase by agreeing to buy at the price of $5 million. We might have been able to get it for less, but as it turned out we did not.

Why could the balance of the purchase price not have been included in the estimates for 1955? Then the house would have known exactly what the deal was. If this practice is followed by the government in other cases we have no possible way of checking these purchases. If buildings are going to be bought with moneys taken out of a vote covering 20 other buildings, how is it going to be possible for members of parliament to make an adequate check of these transactions?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I quite agree that this is the type of thing one should avoid if one can, not that there is anything wrong in it, but if you can have an orderly purchase of property through the public works branch for a 12-month period, well and good. However, I would think that hon. members would not suppose that we would close our minds and our thoughts to purchasing property in any period other than in September, October and November when the estimates are made up for a given year. When the item of $1 million was drawn to the attention of hon. members in the supplementary estimates last year they were asked to vote for the purchase of this

Supply-Public Works particular property. I agree that because of the fact negotiations were continuing it was not possible to disclose the purchase price, and I do not think the minister who presented the item to the committee did in fact do so.
As I say, the purchase price had not been negotiated so that to that extent hon. members might very well say that they voted $1 million thinking that the purchase price was going to be $2 million. I agree that is one criticism that can be directed at this particular item. On the other hand, hon. members are now being given the item with all the details of the purchase. If they feel that $5 million is not the proper price to be paid for the property they have precisely the same right as they would have had if the item had appeared in the blue book.
Oh, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Oh, yes. That is the situation. As I say, I would hope that we would not do this too often. I would hope that you could have orderly planning.
How many times have you done it in the last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: So far as I know, we have not done it at all. I would hope that it will not happen, but here it is. Nevertheless, there is no difference in virtue between a supplementary estimate authorizing the purchase of a building and an item in the main estimates. It does the same thing, as my hon. friend knows.

Why would it not have been fairer to the house if the whole balance of the purchase price had been included in this supplementary estimate rather than picking up $2i million, half of the total price, from a vote covering other buildings?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

speechtext:
We were told last year by the Minister of Public Works that he had taken a broom and cleaned up his department; we were going to have a new deal in the Department of Public Works. They were only going

to call for money to be voted that they would spend, and yet in his own department apparently we have the one case where they picked up $2-5 million out of a vote which was supposed to cover other buildings and used that money rather than put it in the estimates and have it brought before parliament. Surely the Minister of Finance does not condone procedure of that kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I think we are disagreeing, Mr. Chairman, and I hesitate to say it again, on the timing. This is the only occasion on which we could vote this money. We could not have put it in the blue book until the transaction was completed and part of the purchase price paid. Even if you forget for a moment the $2 [DOT] 5 million, we have already paid $1 million, and the purchase is in fact authorized. We have an outstanding agreement of sale from last summer bearing interest at 5 per cent. The sooner the money is paid the more interest we will save. Surely, the only way to do it is to bring it forward into the supplementary estimates, get the money and pay it on the purchase price to complete the transaction.
Why did we vote the $1 million?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I think the $1 million probably could have been in the $3 [DOT] 5 million, but once again it is a case of voting enough to secure a contract and not enough to make the purchaser feel he is getting all he is asking.
The purchase had not been made.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
No, the purchase had not been made. We had an offer then from the owner of the property and we were engaged in negotiations which would lead to purchase. We had to have money to make a down payment if we got an agreement, and that is what, in fact, the $1 million was intended for.
If my hon. friend will forgive me, if we voted this in the main estimates for this coming year, we might not pass that item for some time to come. At any rate, it is not something for the future, it is something in the past; it is done. The arrangements have been made. This is just like every other item; it is to clean up existing obligations of the government of Canada.

Did the Minister of Finance know that the Department of Public Works had picked up $2-5 million to apply on the purchase price of this building by getting it from the moneys voted for other buildings?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The answer is yes, Mr. Chairman. The Minister of Finance was the chairman of a meeting of treasury board that authorized this manner of dealing with the subject.
Was the $2 million the net down payment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No, the down payment was $1 million. We are speaking now of the $2-5 million.
I know you are.

The Minister of Finance was a party to this transaction, then, of taking the $2 [DOT] 5 million from the other vote in public works and applying it on the purchase price of this building, without bringing the expenditure to parliament; is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I hope the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra does not think I am so simple as to fall into a trap like that.
It is no trap; it is a fact.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The Minister of Finance
authorized the payment on the property which had already been purchased by agreement on which a payment of $1 million had been made as a down payment, consequent upon parliament having passed it. Now, without the item in the supplementary estimates of last May or June there would have been no subsequent payment because parliament had not authorized the purchase.
The minister did not seem to know anything about this $2-5 million last Friday night when we were asking about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: As I said a moment ago, that was my fault. I had the figure in front of me and I did not read it out. I accept full responsibility for not explaining the method of financing this building until this moment.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I should like to say a further word regarding this $2-5 million. As I understand it, when parliament passed item 369 in the estimates for the year which ends tomorrow, it was under the usual provision that that money was to be spent as detailed in the back of the book, with the usual statutory provision that if any changes in those details were to be made they had to be submitted to and approved by the treasury board. The Minister of Finance now indicates that was done. I suggest that there must have been some pretty clear-cut report or recommendation laid before the treasury board. There must have been a formal minute which would indicate how it came about that out of a vote of $10,640,000, there was spare money to the tune of $2-5 million.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra made a guess that was fairly accurate; he said there were about 20 buildings here and I count 21, so that is getting pretty close. They varied in amounts from $50,000 for the construction of a parking area north of Wellington Street to a vote of $2,400,000 for
Supply-Public Works a food and drug laboratory for the Department of National Health and Welfare. I believe that was built. As I look over these estimates, it seems to me that something was done on most of them. What I am trying to do now is set out what I believe to be the picture, and I believe I have stated it correctly. I am asking the minister to produce, if he cannot do it today he can table it in the house very soon, the minute of treasury board and the recommendations dealing with this matter so we will know just how it was that $2-5 million was saved out of this item. He should let us know the secret as to which of these items was not spent or was underspent. Surely the treasury board, of which the Minister of Finance was chairman at the time, did not pass this minute without knowing what it was doing. How about letting us know what was done? Will he table this minute of the treasury board?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am glad to tell my hon. friend the date on which the treasury board changed the $2-5 million, and I can assure him now, and will give him any evidence he wants, that treasury board does not act on those things until there is a recommendation that, in fact, there is a deficiency in the vote and these moneys can be used for that purpose.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I do not want to be obnoxious about this, but it does seem to me we have a right to see that minute of treasury board. In fact, it is pretty near to an order in council. I believe that it has the same status as an order in council. It is a little different from the ordinary order in council in that automatic publication is not required. Surely these matters are not secret. This makes me wonder how many other instances there may be where the details in the back of the book have been altered after the item has been voted by parliament, as laid down in the Financial Administration Act. I am ready to admit that is provided for by law. When we pass an item in the front of the book, the details at the back of the book are mainly for our information, but it is more than that. The money is to be spent as provided in the details, unless the government wants to make a change which it can do by application to the treasury board. Surely that application must include all the facts. Surely we are entitled to those facts.
The minister nods his head, but that is not recorded in Hansard. I ask again, can this minute be tabled?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Certainly.

I want to ask a couple of questions here. The minister

Supply-Public Works said the decision to buy this building was not made until a year ago. However, back in 1952 according to the public accounts some $203,000 was spent on repairs and alterations to that building. Now, were any other repairs and alterations besides that $203,000 made?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Did my hon. friend say $303,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: My notes say that we spent $247,305.
This would be spent in 1952?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is the grand total in repairs and alterations.
Was any consideration given, in the final figure, on account of those payments, and these alterations?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, we took it into account in considering the valuation of the $5 million on the other building we are buying.
They never gave consideration in regard to the rentals.

One of the most serious aspects of the situation seems to be that in June of last year we received assurances from the Minister of Public Works that in the future there was to be no inflation in his estimates. Yet, two months later, in this one item, they are able to collect 25 per cent of the amount authorized for expenditure in Ottawa. Surely there is a case in which there was very definite inflation of the estimates. Within two months of the passing of the estimates in the House of Commons he was able to collect $2,500,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I did not say that. August, 1954, is the treasury board minute authorizing the purchase of the building. That was not the date on which the $2,500,000 was transferred.
When was this money made available? The minister told me, if I heard him correctly, that it was made available in August of last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, but that was the date of the purchase agreement. Is the hon. member asking when the $2,500,000 was paid?
Yes, when the $2,500,000 was paid.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Well, $1 million of it was paid, or authorized, on September 30, and $1,500,000 on February 11.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Two separate treasury board minutes?
[Mr. Fraser (Peterborough) .1

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.
Is it not a fact that this $2,500,000 that was not spent on other buildings was used on this one so as to save interest?
Oh, oh.
To save face.
It does appear, Mr. Chairman, that this is a very irregular way of doing business.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Perfectly regular.

It is irregular, despite what the hon. member for Fort William has said. I note that the minister says it is entirely regular. Well, if it is, it is strange that when the government asked us to vote $1 million they must have known what the situation was. Treasury board would not vote $1 million unless they knew what it was for.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Treasury board did not vote it; parliament voted it.
But it was voted, and your intention was to buy the building.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.

The intention was to buy the building at the time. Then, $1 million should not have been voted, unless $5 million was voted. It would not have cost any more, if these moneys had been voted in the regular fashion. Surely, when it is making a purchase, the government does not need to tell the seller that because a vote is passed in parliament the government has to use the total amount when making the purchase.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No, but what vendor would not pay any attention to the vote?

As the hon. member for Simcoe North points out, at the rate the government spends money, sellers know that you do not need to pay out all that is voted. I know the minister has lived in a rural district and traded horses, and he will know that you do not-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I know my hon. friend trades them, and he never tells in advance what he is going to pay for an animal, so that that information gets to the ears of the man who is selling it.

No, but I will say this to the minister, that nobody has ever charged me $1,000 more for a horse, merely because he thought that that meant I had $1,500 more in my pocket.
Nobody is going to sell anything to the government of Canada without knowing he is going to get paid for it. No salesman expects that the minister, spending upwards of $5

billion each year, is not going to have enough to pay for an item like this. If it was the intention, as it appears to have been, to pay that amount, then it should have been voted as $5 million. And if it required only $4,500,000 it would be easy to come back and say that in the vote of $5 million you had $500,000 more than you needed.
And so I think we should have the information asked for by the hon. member from Winnipeg. We should have the details. I am glad to hear the minister admit that it must be irregular, because it had not happened before. And I think he has given the intimation today that he does not intend to let it happen again. In any event we would hope that it would not happen again. While I am casting no reflection upon the integrity of any of the parties to the deal, and while I am not questioning the value-I am not arguing whether it is worth $5 million or $5,500,000 or $4,500,000 or $7 million; you may have got a bargain; we do not know about that- I certainly do feel that this is a very irregular procedure. It is unfair to the opposition, unfair to parliament and unfair to the taxpayers to make a deal in the way this one was made.
The minister seems to imply that it would have made some difference had the vendor known that a vote for $5 million had been passed. But surely that would not affect the price of the building. The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich points out that you had $2,500,000 that you picked up from somewhere else. We do not know what other building that was dropped from, but we do know there was $2,500,000 from somewhere. If you had been aboveboard in stating what it was to be spent for it would not have cost any more. I think we should be told what other building suffered, if any did suffer. And if no other building suffered, then you voted $2,500,000 you should not have voted in the first place.
I do not think we should hold up the item indefinitely. It is a matter that can be regretted, and I think the government more or less admits that its procedure has been a bit irregular.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I have not said that.

No, I know the minister has not. He says he is not going to be led into any trap, by admitting anything. Somebody says that it is not a trap, that it is a fact. Whether you admit it or not, the fact is that we say this was highly irregular.

In addition to tabling the minute of treasury board which, I understand, the minister has agreed to do, would he also table the lease agreement and the sale agreement, as well as the evaluation certificates?
Supply-Public Works

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Before we go further, of course I have no objection to the tabling of all these papers in the normal way. I would not wish to undertake to do it myself, but I presume the Minister of Public Works, or whoever negotiated the transaction, would do it. I can give the details of the lease, and the bare fact that $5 million was the purchase price. I do not know of there being any arrangements other than that. If my hon. friend wants to have the papers, I would have no objection.
But I have one word to say about the treasury board item. I regret I shall have to inform the committee that it has not been the custom to table treasury board minutes. I was not aware of that a moment ago. I am prepared to answer any questions asked, but I gather that the tabling of treasury board minutes is not done.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Is it because of custom that it is not done, or is it prohibited by law, or is this part of the veil of secrecy?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: As hon. members know, treasury board is in fact a committee of cabinet, and the only results of cabinet meetings which are tabled are orders in council. Under those conditions I cannot table it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I must say I have seen such things tabled as minutes of treasury board. Now, whether there were various categories I do not know. If that cannot be done, will the minister answer a question if someone puts it on the order paper-I can think of someone who will-as to what happened to the details of this particular vote? Which of the items were spent in full, which were not spent at all, and which were spent in part? How did $2,500,000 come to be saved?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, I shall get that information.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That set of questions will be on the order paper shortly.
On an item of $5 million we have two appraisers acting for this government and on behalf of the taxpayers of Canada. There is a difference of $500,000.
I am taking the minister's word, although I do not believe it is very accurate. I am willing to take his word, but I have another figure of around $900,000.
That is what he said.
If that is what he said my hearing is not any better than a lot of your statements. There is a difference of $900 million.

It is $900,000.

Supply-Public Works

I got that from the Minister of Trade and Commerce; what's a million here or there? If the minister were doing business for himself or the Minister of Public Works were doing business for himself, if he were buying a piece of property for around $5 million and obtained two appraisals on the building in which there was a difference of $900 million-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It is not $900 million.

No, $900,000. I would think the first thing he would do would be to say there is something radically wrong here. I am going to call in competent appraisers. Certainly one of these firms is crazy or has made a great error. But no, that is not the way this government does business. That is not a sufficiently large figure to stop them in their tracks from purchasing the building and seeking the correct value somewhere else. They say one firm says so and so and another firm says something else, and there is a difference of $900,000. What does that amount to? After all, the ministers are just human beings. Do not lose sight of the usual practice of human beings in transacting business, because any human being in the world in charge of a transaction of this magnitude would be struck dumb with a difference of $900,000 in the evaluations.
I am going to ask some friends of mine who are doing federal government contract work to give me a figure at which they would be glad to tender on a similar building, to give me a figure they would be glad to submit in this day and age when construction costs have risen above what they were when the government purchased the building. I believe we still might find, and I believe the government would be glad to know, that they should not be so foolish as to be stampeded into buying this building to provide the accommodation they need. They rush into it. They obtain two evaluations. There is a difference of $900,000 in the figures. They say they have to get this money; there has to be the utmost secrecy in the whole transaction, or the vendor will not sell us the most valuable piece of property in Canada. We will take a five-year lease with the vendor-how long was the lease? Was it five years?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes. If my hon. friend is saying we had this property then he is quite wrong.
You needed the building and you leased it for five years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.

That was not satisfactory. You had plenty of time to erect a building at proper costs before you closed this deal.


If you had done that you would not be guessing at where you stand today. The public of Canada would know where they were heading, and they would not be guessing at the course you have taken.

Apparently I am a little unusual, Mr. Chairman. I am still interested in the value of this building and the price paid for it. I notice that in the public accounts for 1953, volume I, at page V-8, it is indicated that 269,000 square feet of space were occupied in this building. I also notice that the minister indicated at page 2425 of Hansard that 229,500 square feet were occupied. Does this mean that the space leased was greater than the space purchased?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No. The simple explanation is that the larger figure is the gross area; the smaller figure is the net that is used.

These figures would indicate that in Ottawa the purchase price is high and the rental is fairly reasonable. In connection with the observations of the hon. member for Simcoe North, may I ask whether this figure was arrived at simply by an offer from the vendor, or was it simply a split the difference transaction between two evaluations, or how was the figure of $5 million arrived at?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The $5 million was arrived at by the usual process of having evaluations and having the department itself come to the conclusion that the purchase price was fair, after all the investigation of the building as to its value, as to its usefulness to the government, and so on.
In connection with the evaluation, I think the minister said that he had no access to the cost of this building. I think he indicated that by nodding his head.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I do not understand what the hon. member is saying now.
The minister had no indication of the actual building costs, because he did not put up the building.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No, I did not say that. I said I did not have them. I presume the Department of Public Works has them.
