Did the government have an indication of the actual amount spent by the vendor to put up the building?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I would doubt very much whether the vendor of a building would disclose to a would-be purchaser the cost of that building.
That may be true, but in connection with the closing of this transaction I assume the minister had a statement of adjustments of some kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Not until we get this money to close the deal.
It is still not closed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No.
Has there been any indication to the government that there are any arrears on mortgages on the property, or of liens filed against the property.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Not that I know of.
Has there been any indication that the vendor has taken care of the outside purchase price and has paid all bills?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: If he has not they will be deducted on the completion of the transaction, in the usual legal way.

That may be so;
but his reasons for selling or the price he might have to get may have some bearing on that.

The minister has told us there were two appraisal firms and there was a difference of $900,000 in their evaluations. Can the minister give us the names of the two appraisal firms and the evaluation set by each, and also when they were given?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I have not the dates. The appraisers were E. S. Sherwood of Ottawa and J. E. Pitt of Montreal. The Sherwood appraisal was $4,491,750 and the Pitt appraisal, the higher one, was $5,386,242.
Can the minister say whether the government put a heating system in this building, and if so, what was the cost?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am not aware of the government putting in a heating system.
I understood they did.
Can the minister tell the committee the fees paid to these two firms that appraised the building?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No, but I shall get that for the hon. member.

I have a question on item 369 out of which I understood the minister said the $2,500,000 was taken to complete the purchase price. In this item there is $150,000 for improved accommodation for the R.C.M.P. at the seminary building. Was that $150,000 spent in addition to the $2,500,000?
Supply-Public Works

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The $150,000 is what I gave a moment ago, and then there is $247,000 for additions and repairs.
What money has been spent on the upkeep of the grounds, landscaping and work of that kind? This property comprises some 113 acres.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We have no property yet; we have not spent any money except the amount of $247,000 I have given.
Is there anything in the estimates for the next fiscal year covering an expenditure of that kind or of any other kind in connection with this building?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I shall let my hon. friend know in a minute.
I think this is a case where the Minister of Public Works could well have been here this afternoon, on an important item like this.

I understood the minister to say that what one might call the cost over and above the purchase price of $5 million, or rather the expenditure by the government over and above the $5 million, amounted to approximately $449,000 paid as rent, $56,000 paid as interest, $247,000 for alterations, and then there was a vote of $150,000 to which the hon. member for Victoria (Ont.) referred and which was covered by vote No. 369 of last year, which was described by Hon. Mr. Fournier as being absolutely necessary for the efficient operation of the headquarters and to take care of normal expansion requirements. That adds up to about $900,000 over and above the purchase price. Am I right in saying that is what it cost the government in addition to the purchase price? Are there any other expenditures in connection with the building which have not been taken into account in the discussion today?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I think the $150,000 referred to by the hon. member for Victoria, Ont., is part of the total expenditure of $247,000 which I gave. To answer my hon. friend, the expected cost of valuations, surveyor fees and legal fees is $20,000.
Is the minister tabling the lease and the sale agreement?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, I will do that.
I think we should tidy this up a little bit before we finish. The purchase price was $5 million and now we have added to that nearly $900,000.

No.

Supply-Public Works

Half a million for rent, a quarter of a million for something else; $150,000 for repairs. That is $900,000 according to my figures, although it may be up or down $2. That brings it pretty close to the $6 million mark. This big building is not adequate for the mounted police requirements, is that not right?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It is very suitable.

In 1953 when they moved in it was said that this was not big enough or was not adequate. Even yet all the mounted police and their equipment are not out there. You are still renting space in the city of Ottawa. Are you going to build more buildings out there?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We have 988 people in the building. Should it be necessary to provide for another 1,000 people some day no doubt we will do so.
You are still paying rentals in the city of Ottawa for the R.C.M.P.?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There is hardly a department of government which is not located in three or four different buildings in Ottawa. We have never been able to find money to provide separate buildings for all departments and I do not suppose we ever shall, except in the case of veterans affairs and their new building. It seems to be the lot of the civil service and the government to have departments divided up all the time.

In November, 1953, the
Department of Public Works had this to say:
It will be larger than the present temporary headquarters building, running to around 260,000 square feet of space, and designed to accommodate all branches of the force, including stores, which are still located in rented quarters in downtown Ottawa.
Adjoining the new headquarters will be a housing development for members of the force, and shops, stores and other subsidiary buildings.
The present temporary headquarters building was occupied by the force only a few months ago but already is inadequate. Halls and passages are used for filing cases and records and the building is not the most suitable . . .
What has the minister to say to that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: As I said before, personally I am happy that we are spending $5 million, or $6 million if you like, rather than building a new building. I think these quarters are much better than the quarters the police had before and I think they will do for some time to come. The time will come, no doubt, when it will get so crowded that we will have to find another building, but I do not suppose I shall be around at that time.
This building is' not adequate now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I do not admit that. This
building is doing the work for practically all the R.C.M.P. except for some storage space for goods of one kind and another in downtown Ottawa. There is no reason in the world why that storage space should not be downtown instead of out at this particular building. Perhaps it would be more convenient if it were out there, but once again there is a great deal of inconvenience in these things and one has to put up with it. I doubt very much if we will be able to build a special building for the R.C.M.P. for some time to come.

Is it the intention of the department to use the 100 acres of extra land purchased with this building for a housing project or for future additions, or is it the intention of the department to dispose of this land, which might reduce the cost?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No. The moneys which my hon. friend was referring to were in connection with a new building project.
It did not go with this building? I thought it went with this building.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We bought 113 acres with the building, but the money the hon. member referred to, to build a new building and a housing development in connection with it, was not this project.
What are you going to do with the land?
That was in your estimate of $10 million.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I have not an estimate of $10 million.

The other day the public works department estimated $10 million for the over-all picture. You still have buildings rented downtown and will have for years to come. This building is not adequate. There is no force or organization in Canada that needs proper attention and care and proper housing more than the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. I think it is a mistake for the government to go ahead and buy a building which is not adequate for the force. The R.C.M.P. are going to be increasing by leaps and bounds because province after province is doing away with its provincial police and turning things over to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
This is just like building a post office which is too small in the beginning. You are not planning for the future at all. In future years we may have an estimate for the construction of another building alongside this one, and the result will be a mixed up, jumbled affair. I suppose we will have to

follow the late Mr. Mackenzie King's policy and wait and see what is going to happen. The fact is that this building is inadequate, and the minister knows it.

I might say it was not adequate at the time, because Hon. Mr. Fournier, the then minister of public works, stated in answer to a question asked by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra that they were going to construct an additional building to cost $150,000. Mr. Fournier at that time said this:

Even at that, when they moved out of the justice building and went over there, they still found that they did not have sufficient space. They made this request to the Department of Public Works to furnish them with another 12,500 feet. So this building, I am told, will not be of a permanent character as are the buildings you have on Wellington street, like the veterans' building or the justice building. It will be to complete the space that they need for their operations.
At that time the space was not adequate. They asked for an additional 12,500 feet, and that was several years ago, in 1953, when they were merely renting the property. I imagine that today they are still cramped.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: As I say, we have spent $247,000 in making the building more adaptable to their needs. But I can assure hon. members that at this moment I know of no request from the R.C.M.P. for a new building of that nature.
Earlier this afternoon the minister referred to garages. Are there garages on this property?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.
There are garages constructed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.
Adequate in number?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am told so.
What part of the establishment is housed at Rockcliffe? Is there not part of the establishment out at Rockcliffe yet?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There will be establishments of a small nature, of course, here and there in order to be located closer to the work they are dealing with. But this is the headquarters of the R.C.M.P.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, since the last time I was on my feet I have managed to draft the questions that I suggested I would put on the order paper, and they will appear in print tomorrow. In the meantime it seems to me that this whole question has raised an issue even more important than the particular item of expenditure we have been discussing.
Supply-Public Works
It has been clearly brought out that there was this amount of $2,500,000 which was paid by saving it out of item 369 of the estimates of 1954-55. The minister at first seemed to think I had made a reasonable request when I asked for the tabling of the minutes of treasury board making that alteration. He now tells me, or rather he told me later, that it is not the custom to table such minutes.
I have been looking through the Financial Administration Act to see if I can find any authority for withholding such minutes, and I have been unable to find any such authority. It might be there, but as yet it has escaped my notice, at any rate. However, in the Financial Administration Act there is section 29, which is pertinent to this discussion. It comes under part III of the act which is headed "Public Disbursements". After all, this is a fairly important activity of government over which there is laid down strict parliamentary control. Section 29 reads as follows:
At the commencement of each fiscal year or at such other times as the treasury board may direct, the deputy head or other officer charged with the administration of a service for which there is an appropriation by parliament or an item included in estimates then before the House of Commons shall prepare and submit to the treasury board through the comptroller a division of such appropriation or item into allotments in the form detailed in the estimates submitted to parliament for such appropriation or item-
It is quite clear that the deputy minister is required to submit to treasury board the details of an item in the form in which they are set out in the back of the book. In other words we rely on it when we pass an item, that the intention is to spend it as set out in the back of the book. The section continues: -or in such other form as the board may prescribe, and when approved by the board the allotments shall not be varied or amended without the approval of the board, and the expenditures charged to the appropriation shall be limited to the amounts of such allotments.
I think I was perfectly fair in my previous statement when I recognized the fact that the department has the right, under the statute, to request a variation in the details. But that variation cannot be made unless it is approved by the treasury board. But I submit that two-thirds of this blue book of estimates becomes a mockery if these details can be altered time and again without our being able to get the minutes of treasury board which indicate such changes as have been made.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that this matter now goes a great deal further than the question of this particular expenditure now before us. As I indicated a moment ago, I have taken the minister's suggestion and have submitted order paper questions which I trust will get the information we want with respect

Supply-Public Works to this particular item. But I ask the minister to consider further the seriousness of his statement that it is not the custom to table these minutes.
I am the last one to suggest that every last minute of treasury board or every last little order in council or regulation that is passed should be tabled. The table would not hold them. Everyone knows that there is a great deal of detail that is routine and administrative, about which we do not need to be concerned. It may also be true that there may be alterations in details of expenditures which are minor and about which we do not need to be unduly exercised. But surely we should have the right at any time to have brought down before the House of Commons a minute of treasury board altering any of the details that are set out in the back of the book of estimates.
I give as my authority for that submission section 29 of the Financial Administration Act, to which I have just referred. I realize that perhaps the minister is not now in a position to look up the authorities to find out why this custom has been as it is, but I seriously ask him to review the statement he made to me a few minutes ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I shall do so, Mr. Chairman, and I shall be prepared to discuss the matter on my own estimates.

I have one more question, Mr. Chairman, and then I am through. The government purchased 114 acres in this property out there. Will the minister say what they are going to do with all this land? Is it going to be space for officials and officers of the R.C.M.P.?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The present intention is not to sell the land but to retain it as part of the federal district authority. If, however, additions to this building should be needed from time to time in order to house additional staff, if that can be done effectively and efficiently, it will be done; and we shall continue to have this as a good headquarters for the R.C.M.P.

The minister says this land is to be retained as part of the federal district commission over-all picture. Is that his own opinion or is it according to the planning of the commission? Are we to believe that from now on if we purchase a building or make some deal with regard to a building with 100 acres attached, whether it is in accordance or in keeping with the general over-all plan, if there is around there a 100-acre area more or less that cost $2,500,000, we will just keep it too? Does the minister know for a positive

fact that it is part of the plan to retain that property? He spoke with authority.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the great difficulty one always has when dealing with vacant land which is expensive is this. If you dispose of it, in a few years you may regret it because you will need it for other purposes. If you dispose of it you can no longer have a certain amount of park land in a heavily populated city. In this particular case, holding the land has two virtues. The first is that some day we may feel that we have to add to this building, and add to it substantially. We may also have to erect other buildings as they are needed, if we have room on this ground. In the meantime it is desirable to hold it as part of the long-term buildup of the federal district area and it will be suitable, during the period of time that is desirable. Ultimately it would no doubt be used as commercial property, either by government or otherwise.

From the point of view of ordinary common-sense business methods, does the minister not hope for the sake of the taxpayers of Canada that there will not be many more such purchases involving an excess amount of land, certainly to the extent of 80 acres? If the government purchased 100 similar properties with the same amount of land would the minister still think it would be advisable to retain the extra 80 acres whether or not the government knew what it was going to do with it, and pay out the taxpayers' money in that way? Does the minister sincerely believe the statement he has just made, that they are going to hold the land because they are not sure what they are going to do with it and, although it has been purchased with the taxpayers' money, they are going to hold it because they may want to use it for a building or as park land? It may be required for a polo park.
We have purchased it, and the minister says when we did so we intended to get a building large enough to accommodate the mounted police adequately. That was the reason the building was purchased. It was not a venture on which money might be made or lost as holders of land on behalf of the taxpayers. The purpose was purely and simply to purchase a building because there was dire necessity for it to house the mounted police. We have done that. Now the minister comes along and says they are going to keep the land because it may be needed for a park or for expansion. We do not know what it will be used for. But that is what we are spending the taxpayers' money on, and it is a most improbable proposition when we do not know definitely what is going to be done with it.

We are putting the taxpayers of Canada into the real estate business. That is what we are doing.
Would the minister say a building could not have been designed specifically for the needs of the mounted police and constructed for $6 million or less on an adequate amount of ground?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am not a builder and I could not say that. What I have said is that both on the basis of the valuations received and on the basis of the judgment of the Department of Public Works, who are charged with the responsibility of making the decision for the government of Canada, it was thought that this building at $5 million and the additions that have been made to it would be suitable for the purpose. It was also decided, as I have already indicated, that it was preferable to buy the building at that time rather than design and wait for the completion of a building which might cost more. As a matter of fact I still rely on the hon. member for Victoria, Ont., who has quoted from a document indicating that such a building would cost $10 million.

Does the minister not think it would have been desirable to have the Department of Public Works look into the question and find out if it would have been possible to design a building specifically for the needs of the mounted police, rather than put the mounted police in a building which admittedly is not altogether suitable for their needs, and that could have been improved upon if a building had been designed specifically for the purpose?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I have said before that the
ideal would be to design a building for a particular purpose every time, but we cannot achieve the idea. We try to get something less than that and get value for our money. I suggest to the committee that that will always be the viewpoint. Certainly in this case it was. I am quite prepared to agree with my hon. friend that a building for the R.C.M.P. could have been designed which would not have been the same as this building. There is no question about that. But, as I say, the people we have on our payroll who are charged with the responsibility of making such decisions decided that this building was suitable and valuable at that price. If they are not acting wisely and giving proper advice to the government in the discharge of their duties I would listen to a suggestion from my hon. friend that we might dispense with their services, but I have faith that these people do not make these decisions without careful consideration.
Supply-Public Works

But the minister admits he did not get an alternative price. He did not find out how much it would cost to design and construct a building specifically for the purpose of the mounted police. He did not explore the alternative. He took the recommendation of the valuators that this building would probably do and that the mounted police could get along with it, but he did not explore the possibility of securing for the mounted police exactly what they required and finding out how much that would cost.

Mr. Chairman, I was all
through but the minister has tried to put words in my mouth. He said that I said a building costing $10 million was required. I do not know whether those were his exact words, but may I say that so far as I am concerned there is nothing too good for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Their numbers are increasing all the time, and we certainly need them. However, when I referred to the figure of $10 million I said for that amount you could have a much better building than the present one and could also construct a housing project for all the officers and officials who go with the mounted police.
This may not be a bad deal. I do not know, and I am not prepared to say. It may be a good deal, but you have not an adequate building for the mounted police. There was plenty of time to build a new building after this one was rented, if the department had seen fit to do so.
I do not like the minister to say that I suggested a building costing $10 million. I do not suggest that the government should spend a dollar more than it has to, but when you are constructing a building and spending money it may be better to look ahead a little and spend $10 million now for a suitable building. You will need the 114 acres; don't worry about that. 1 would gamble money- I will spend the odd dollar that way any time-that within four or five years you will decide you have made a bad deal because you will have to construct another building costing $5 million before adequate accommodation is provided for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
I should like to ask the hon. member a question.
You do not have to answer questions.
Has he ever seen the building?
Yes, I have seen the building.

speechtext: Item agreed to.

In the new building.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.
The number is increasing all the time?

626.	To provide, subject to regulations of the treasury board, for working capital advances in the current and subsequent fiscal years to posts and employees on posting abroad, and to authorize the creation of a special account in the consolidated revenue fund to which shall be charged such advances and to which shall be credited ex-
(Mr. Hodgson.l
penditures made by and advances recovered from the said posts and employees, the excess of the amounts charged over the amounts credited to the account at any time not to exceed $230,000.

There are one or
two observations I should like to make and one or two questions I should like to ask. The minister has said this afternoon that the function of these further supplementary estimates is to catch up during the course of the fiscal year on payments which it was found necessary to make over and above those provided in the main estimates for specific items. Here we find that he is providing funds both for current advances and subsequent advances. This in fact, I submit, represents a change of policy, and the time for changes of policy to be considered is when the main estimates are before us, not when we are considering supplementary or further supplementary estimates. I suggest to the minister that this item should not be appearing in these further supplementary estimates at all, but should be appearing in the estimates for the coming fiscal year.
My second observation is that it also covers subsequent fiscal years, and that is worse. That figure should, ih fact, also appear in the estimates for 1955-56. I would be glad if the minister would advise the committee as to the reasons for this change in policy being made in this manner.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I agree partially with what my hon. friend has said, Mr. Chairman. However, my remarks as to the purpose of the final supplementary estimates were not to be taken as an exclusive definition of every item that could appear. As he knows quite well, we cannot let the treasury board and its officials cease to work when the blue book is brought out. In this particular case, and I confess it without any difficulty, it was not decided upon at the time the main estimates were certified by me in late December.
Subsequent to that time it was decided to carry a revolving fund of this kind for the immigration people. Now then, there is a choice, either to put it in here when it should get dealt with at the earliest possible moment, or leave it until next year when it would appear in the main estimates. There seems to be no particular point in waiting. This is a principle which has already been approved by parliament. We have these revolving funds for persons who are far away from Ottawa and who need money for the purposes set out in the fund. We do it in external affairs, for example, and for that reason we are asking that we may be permitted to do it with respect to immigration personnel.
Do 1 understand that this policy was decided upon subsequent to the time the blue book for the coming year was printed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

speechtext:
['As one member of the committee, Mr. Chairman, I should like to see this bill go through the house as quickly as possible, but I am reasonably sure we are not going to get it through tonight. I have a few comments to make with respect to war veterans allowances.
The witnesses who appeared before the committee for the Canadian Legion and the national council of veterans in Canada in my judgment made one of the most reasonable presentations that has ever been made to any committee of which I have been a member. In fact their presentation was very temperate. In my opinion they did not ask for anything they could not have been given without any great strain on the treasury.', 'In my opinion this veterans affairs committee has lost its original function. The original function that it used to perform in years gone by was that when veterans legislation was referred to it, the committee had the privilege of opening up the old acts and relating them to the new forces. Back in the 1940's it was a committee that could initiate action and advise the Department of Veterans Affairs on veterans problems. It was a committee in which there was little political bickering. The members were unanimous in their efforts to get the best possible deal for the veterans. But in the last five years I have seen a complete change in the complexion of the committee. Today the government drafts a bill and decides upon policy. The committee has now deteriorated into the position of merely examining the legislation.
I feel sorry for the government members on the committee, because they are placed in the position of having the cabinet make a decision and then being told, "This is what you are going to get." It is put in the form of a bill. Opposition members are at least free to express their opinion and say the things that should be said about certain sections of the bill, but in the last five years government members have been placed in the position that they are not free to get up and argue and express their opinions without being charged with disloyalty to the party or to the government. I feel that the committee is not performing the function it was intended to perform when it was first inaugurated as a non-partisan committee. Then the committee had the right to examine legislation and make recommendations.
I recall occasions upon which the committee had the minister running back and forward to the cabinet day after day, week after week, getting a lot of beneficial changes made. I do not believe that, in so far as some special matters are concerned, the cabinet has all the brains. I do not believe the cabinet has the time to pay attention to different problems, to sit down and study them and decide what is reasonable. I feel this committee on veterans affairs should be a standing committee of the house. It could be called, under the chairmanship of the very capable-parliamentary assistant, to take a look at legislation and decide what should be done. The committee's views could be obtained and taken to cabinet, where they could be looked at and some decision arrived at that would be reasonable. I think the committee are reasonable and fair if they are met half way.
I hope the cabinet will consider the advisability of making that committee a standing

On clause 1-Definitions.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE ALLOWANCES AND PERMISSIBLE INCOME, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when this bill was before the committee of the whole a few days ago I intimated that there were a few remarks I wished to make. As you know, the resolution preceding the bill was debated in the house three weeks ago, and there was also a debate on the motion for second reading. The bill was then sent to the veterans affairs committee which held a number of sittings, during which the principles of the bill were discussed. The bill is now back in the house with very little change as far as the committee is concerned. In fact we could not make any changes, but I believe there is an amendment which will be suggested by the minister.
It will be recalled that the bill provides for a 20 per cent increase in war veterans allowances, bringing the single veteran's allowance from $50 to $60 per month and the married veteran's allowance from $90 to $108. I may say that as far as the committee were concerned this bill might as well have never been sent there, because we were not able to make even any recommendations. However we did have the benefit of briefs presented by the different veterans' organizations such as the Canadian Legion, the national council of veterans' associations in Canada, and other organizations. As usual these briefs and representations were well prepared and quite logical, and I am sure these organizations deserve credit for the presentations they made.
As I have said in this house before, we find that when national veterans' organizations appear before our committee they never exaggerate. They state logically and clearly what they consider to be the requirements and needs of the veterans. As has been said many times in the house, the Canadian veteran has never tried to stampede the electorate or the elected members of the House of Commons into giving him more than he was entitled to. This cannot always be said of veterans in other countries.
We of the opposition were confirmed in the attitude we had taken with respect to Bill No. 164 before it was submitted to the committee. At that time we claimed that it did not go far enough. Along with the veterans we approved the increase from $50 to $60 a month for the single veteran. We all considered that was a step in the right direction, and the government was given approval for having recommended that increase. But the increase from $90 to $108 did not seem to us to be enough, and this also was the opinion of the veterans' organizations. But the chief point of disapproval as far as the

War Veterans Allowance Act bill was concerned was in conection with the ceilings on permissive income. I should like to read from the brief presented on March 11, 1955, to the committee by the Candian Legion, in particular their comments on the ceilings on permissive income, as follows:
Ceilings on permissive income-
Recommendation-
That the ceiling on total permissible income under W.V.A., be increased to $1,200 per year in the case ol a single recipient and $2,000 per year in the case of those married.
Comment-
We must again reiterate that, even if this section of the act is amended as proposed in Bill 164, the act will still tend to defeat its own purpose. If the allowance is intended to assist the aged and needy veteran the low ceilings on permissive income prevent him from supplementing the allowance sufficiently to enjoy a reasonable standard of living.
The national council of veterans' associations in Canada also presented a brief. Both these organizations are nation-wide and represent hundreds of thousands of veterans of both wars. The- recommendation made by this organization contained in the brief presented to the committee on March 14, 1955, was as follows:
That the total annual allowable income including war veterans allowance permitted under the War Veterans Allowance Act be the amount set as statutory exemptions under the Income Tax Act, subject to supplementation of $200 in the case of the single man.
As we know, the exemptions under the Income Tax Act are $1,000 for a single person and $2,000 for a married person. This recommendation amounts to $1,200 for the single man and $2,000 for the married man, and is the same as the recommendation by the Canadian Legion. Their comment on this is as follows:
We note with concern the means test limitations proposed by this bill for the single man is $840 per annum. This would permit only $120 per year or $10 per month through income from earnings or other sources. We consider that the means test for the single man should be at least set at the level of $1,200 which would permit $480 of supplementation.
In the case of the married man who must maintain a home, however modest, we consider that it should be advanced proportionately and suggest again the statutory exemption in respect to income tax, namely $2,000.
There were other recommendations by other veterans' organizations, but these were the main representations in connection with the permissive income. The Legion stated in its brief that the act will still tend to defeat its own purpose. As we understood it, the purpose of the War Veterans Allowance Act was to help those who most needed help. I think it is a fair comment to say that the whole act and the whole veterans allowance regulations are weighted in favour of the veteran who is employable and who is able

to obtain work. The veteran who needs it most, the veteran who is unemployable, is the one who receives the least consideration.
I do not think that is the intention of the War Veterans Allowance Act.
I admit-and it was admitted a few minutes ago-that as far as the allowance is concerned, the single veteran has received fair treatment. As far as the employable veteran is concerned, we acknowledge and admit that he is in a fair position. I say that, Mr. Chairman, taking into consideration the fact that the regulations now permit of a broader- I might almost say generous-interpretation of casual earnings as far as the employable veteran is concerned. As I say, the employable veteran is in a fair position. But as far as these veterans are concerned-and they are mostly veterans of the first war-we must take into consideration that fact that they are old men.
The act was brought into force in 1930. It is 25 years since the War Veterans Allowance Act was first passed. Twenty-five years have been added to the age of these men, many of whom in those days were considered not able to fend for themselves. Hence when I say the position is fair, we must take into consideration first whether the veteran's age permits him to take advantage of casual labour. That is the first consideration. Then there is another "if", and it is a big one, namely if his health permits a man of 67 to do so. That is the average age today, and many are years older than that. Then there is a third "if", namely if there is employment. We have been discussing unemployment in the House of Commons for some days now. When there is much unemployment in the country the man who is least likely to get employment is the old veteran 65, 66 or 67 years of age. In many parts of the country, while he might consider himself to be employable, nevertheless employment is not there for him.
In the committee we tried to find out just how many veterans could take advantage of casual earnings. We have no information as to the number of men. We have information as to the number that take advantage of section 4, which allows a man to take his war veterans allowance by the month and then, when he can get work, to go off the war veterans allowance and take that work. But only some 1,100 out of over 40,000 war veterans were able to take advantage of this section 4.
That is a fact which indicates that there - are very few war veterans today who can take advantage of the type of work permitted under section 4. I will venture to say that

the number who are able to take casual employment would turn out to be extremely disappointing to our hopes.
As I just stated, if the employable veteran can get employment, and if his health permits it, he is very well looked after. But this legislation does not help the unemployable veteran, the man who really needs the war veterans allowance more than any other veteran.
First, we have the man with a small pension, say of $25 a month. The ceiling is $70 a month. The war veterans allowance he would receive would not be $60 a month but would be only $45 a month, and the total income he would have would be $840 a year.
Then there is the veteran who has worked, has been thrifty and has been able to lay aside enough to purchase an annuity which brings him $20, $25 or $30 a month. He is in exactly the same position as the veteran with the disability pension. The ceiling for him is again $70 a month, and that man has to live on $840 a year.
Then again there is the veteran who has reached the age of 70. While every other man in Canada over the age of 70 years can take full advantage of the $40 monthly which the law allows him, as well as of whatever other income he has-whether it be $100, $1,000, $10,000 or more he can take full advantage of that income-the war veteran over 70 years of age is given the $40 old age security but his ceiling again is $70 a month and he is permitted to receive only $30 out of the $60 allowed him for war veterans allowance.
As to the unemployable veterans who are obliged to live on their very small pensions, who cannot go out and seek casual labour,
I say this act discriminates against them to a great extent.
During the sittings of the committee there were some members who said-and it was echoed and bandied about from one to another of the government members-that the $70 is not a ceiling but a floor. There is a certain amount of truth in that contention with regard to the employable veteran, the man who least needs the war veterans allowance. But as far as the unemployable veteran is concerned it is indeed a ceiling which cannot be penetrated as far as his income is concerned. To me that argument sounded shallow indeed.
Taking all these things into consideration, Mr. Chairman, and after listening to the Legion and the other veterans' organizations, the opposition members of the committee-and I refer to the official opposition, which was supported by the other opposition members-felt that the unemployable
30, 1955	2557
War Veterans Allowance Act veterans should be assisted. I might also say that in the Legion's brief, when they were recommending assistance, this statement was made:
We would urgently request that this committee recommend to the government the immediate adoption of the following measures:
The measures I read here a few moments ago were the measures they recommended that the committee should recommend to the government; and we thought they should be recommended to the government. We realized that we as a committee had no authority to make variations in any section dealing with money matters, and that the only motion we could make was one requesting the government to consider some increase. The hon. member for Hastings-Frontenac, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, moved the following motion in the committee:
That the committee recommend that the government give consideration to introducing legislation during the present session of parliament which will provide that the maximum of total income, as set out in section 1 of schedule "A" to Bill 164, be increased to $1,200, and that in sections 2 and 3 of said schedule "A" the monthly rate be increased to $120 and the maximum total income be increased to $2,000.
The meaning of this motion is simply that we recommend a ceiling of $1,200 for the single man and $2,000 for the married man, and that instead of a 20 per cent increase in the allowance to $108 per month the increase should be to $120 a month for married men. That was the substance of the recommendation we made, and we thought it would receive favourable consideration in the committee. As I say, the matter was placed before the committee. All members of the official opposition and all members of the other opposition groups supported it. They supported what the Legion and other veterans' organizations that had made a definite study of the situation thought was necessary.
I almost hesitate to state some of the arguments used by hon. members on the government side regarding our recommendation. One was that if it went through it would defeat the bill, and I believe some of them actually persuaded themselves that it might. Another was that we must get the bill through before the 1st of April. They said they had made representations to the government, they knew we could not get any more, and therefore we must hurry this matter through the committee. We were told we must not ask for more. That was the main argument, and it was said that we might lose what we had.
There are other members here who were on previous committees and will recall, as I do, that that was not the attitude of the

War Veterans Allowance Act committee in 1951 when it was considering increases in disability pensions. We had a bill presented to us at that time which provided for an increase of only 10 per cent. Every member of the committee was indignant that such a suggestion should be placed before a veterans affairs committee. They would not accept it. We told the government so. Resolutions were moved, the government were contacted and they offered an increase of 15 per cent. Again the veterans affairs committee said it was not enough, it was not fair, and the members of the committee demanded reconsideration. The matter was reconsidered and in the final result an increase of 25 per cent was provided instead of the 10 per cent that was first put before the committee.
We thought some such study would have been made by the committee this year. It may be-I do not know-that the amounts of $1,200 and $2,000 are too much. It may be that an allowance of $108 is enough, but no study was made. There is quite a difference between the total income of $720 now permitted a single veteran and the suggestion of $1,200. Some amount in between might have been more appropriate. It could be that $1,000 or $1,500 might have been considered proper, but the matter was never studied. We should have had some evidence.
So far as married veterans are concerned, it may be that the total annual income of $2,000, instead of the $1,440 provided by the bill, requested by the different organizations and by our resolution, was too much. The matter should at least have been studied. We were told, "This is the bill that has been put before you and there is to be no change; you will accept this and this only". That is the ultimatum that was handed to us as members of the veterans affairs committee.
It seemed to some of us that the committee had not been established for the purpose of finding out what was best for the veterans. I thought it was our purpose to study the bill and, if we did not consider it satisfactory, to make recommendations. But I found out that all we were to do was be rubber stamps and approve whatever was put before us. That is why I said at the beginning of my remarks that the veterans affairs committee might as well not have had any meetings at all. The committee held a number of meetings, but all it accomplished was simply to rubber stamp the bill that had been presented by the government.
I do not think it is necessary for me to prolong this argument. I think the house, people across Canada and particularly the veterans must consider that, this is a matter of unfinished business. We waited for three

and a half years for the war veterans allowance bill to be brought before the house to provide the increases which everybody knew were needed, but when we got it we found the amounts were practically the same as before. The allowances were raised 20 per cent, by $120 and $240 respectively. It would appear that we will have to wait another three or four years before these matters are properly adjusted. The war veterans allowance is the only means of livelihood for unemployable veterans without any other income, of whom there are thousands across the country.
When we considered the question of war veterans allowances in 1951 we had much more evidence placed before us on which to base a finding than we had this time. One of the chief yardsticks for determining what the amount of allowances should be was the cost of living at that time. According to the family spending schedule prepared by the Toronto welfare council at that time a veteran with 100 per cent disability and living alone needed $93.34 a month to provide a minimum basis of living. That is what the figure was in 1951, $93.34 for a single veteran. These figures were worked out scientifically by the Toronto welfare council. If $93.34 was needed in 1951, then just as much and more is needed today; but such a man is only to be allowed an income of $70 a month. For a veteran with a wife and no children the estimate worked out by the Toronto welfare council was $153.43, but we are only permitting him an income of $120 a month.
After waiting three years for the veterans affairs committee to be set up we now find that the business we felt we could and should have done has not been done and, as I said a moment ago, as far as the House of Commons is concerned it must certainly be regarded as being in the category of unfinished business.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE ALLOWANCES AND PERMISSIBLE INCOME, ETC.
speechtext:
As one member of the committee, Mr. Chairman, I should like to see this bill go through the house as quickly as possible, but I am reasonably sure we are not going to get it through tonight. I have a few comments to make with respect to war veterans allowances.
The witnesses who appeared before the committee for the Canadian Legion and the national council of veterans in Canada in my judgment made one of the most reasonable presentations that has ever been made to any committee of which I have been a member. In fact their presentation was very temperate. In my opinion they did not ask for anything they could not have been given without any great strain on the treasury.

In my opinion this veterans affairs committee has lost its original function. The original function that it used to perform in years gone by was that when veterans legislation was referred to it, the committee had the privilege of opening up the old acts and relating them to the new forces. Back in the 1940's it was a committee that could initiate action and advise the Department of Veterans Affairs on veterans problems. It was a committee in which there was little political bickering. The members were unanimous in their efforts to get the best possible deal for the veterans. But in the last five years I have seen a complete change in the complexion of the committee. Today the government drafts a bill and decides upon policy. The committee has now deteriorated into the position of merely examining the legislation.
I feel sorry for the government members on the committee, because they are placed in the position of having the cabinet make a decision and then being told, "This is what you are going to get." It is put in the form of a bill. Opposition members are at least free to express their opinion and say the things that should be said about certain sections of the bill, but in the last five years government members have been placed in the position that they are not free to get up and argue and express their opinions without being charged with disloyalty to the party or to the government. I feel that the committee is not performing the function it was intended to perform when it was first inaugurated as a non-partisan committee. Then the committee had the right to examine legislation and make recommendations.
I recall occasions upon which the committee had the minister running back and forward to the cabinet day after day, week after week, getting a lot of beneficial changes made. I do not believe that, in so far as some special matters are concerned, the cabinet has all the brains. I do not believe the cabinet has the time to pay attention to different problems, to sit down and study them and decide what is reasonable. I feel this committee on veterans affairs should be a standing committee of the house. It could be called, under the chairmanship of the very capable-parliamentary assistant, to take a look at legislation and decide what should be done. The committee's views could be obtained and taken to cabinet, where they could be looked at and some decision arrived at that would be reasonable. I think the committee are reasonable and fair if they are met half way.
I hope the cabinet will consider the advisability of making that committee a standing
30. 1955
War Veterans Allowance Act committee of the house. It is about one minute to six, Mr. Chairman, and there are a few more comments I should like to make, so I wonder if we could call it six o'clock.
Clause stands.
Progress reported.
